sections.html:
Sitting on the Rathdrum Prairie in Kootenai County, Post Falls touches the Washington line roughly 20 miles from Spokane. Coeur d'Alene is its neighbor to the east and the Spokane River marks the south. An estimated 46,715 people lived here on July 1, 2025, a 21.0 percent rise over the 38,620 counted in April 2020.

Prices are high by Idaho standards. The 2020 to 2024 survey puts median value for owner-occupied units at $477,400 and median household income at $82,183. Owners occupy 64.1 percent of homes, median gross rent is $1,469, and about 87 percent of residents were in the same house a year earlier, so newcomers tend to stay put.

One house rarely matches the median. With values this high, listing can be the smarter route for a house in good repair, and there is nothing wrong with choosing it.

Four seasons arrive here, and winter brings a lot of snow: about 59.3 inches in an average year against 25.73 inches of all precipitation. December and January lead at roughly 17 to 19 inches each. Temperature records span minus 30 degrees to 109.

  • Roofs carry snow for months, so buyers look at the age and slope of yours.
  • Gutters, downspouts and drainage matter at spring thaw, when snowmelt can reach crawl spaces.
  • Heating and insulation get scrutiny where winters are this snowy.

Work you have put off can pass to the buyer in an as-is sale, so you avoid paying for it before listing.

Interstate 90 runs through the city, linking Spokane on the west with Coeur d'Alene on the east. Idaho 41 meets the interstate east of town and runs 8 miles north to Rathdrum, and US 95 lies about 7 miles east. Spokane International Airport handles air travel. Average commute time is 24.1 minutes.

District 273, the Post Falls School District, runs the public schools: Post Falls Middle School and the elementary schools Greensferry, Mullan Trail, Ponderosa, Prairie View, Seltice, Treaty Rock and West Ridge, plus Frederick Post Kindergarten. Private choices include Classical Christian Academy and Genesis Prep Academy.

Families want to know which elementary school an address feeds. Keep the district's boundary information handy.

Idaho Code section 63-903 sets December 20 as the due date for the full amount of that year's levy. Owners of real property can split it into two halves, with the second due June 20.

WhenWhat happens in Kootenai County
End of MayAssessment notices mailed
Fourth Monday of JuneLast day to appeal to the Board of Equalization
June 20Second half payable
First week of DecemberBills reach owners
December 20Full amount or first half payable

About 45 taxing districts plus several special districts share in your bill.

• A mailed payment needs a USPS postmark dated on or before the due date to count as timely.
  • Owners who cannot pay can ask the Board of County Commissioners about financial hardship relief at (208) 446-1600.
  • Three years of delinquency on real property sends the parcel into the tax deed process, and only paying the third year in full stops it.

Sellers who have fallen behind should care about this rule most. Mention it up front, because the payoff and the closing date both have to work around it. The Kootenai County Treasurer's FAQ and property tax process page cover the details.

Post Falls issues building permits for construction and renovation, and the city's Building page explains the process and codes. Switching a house to another use or occupancy takes a separate permit, which counts if it ever served as an office or a rental.

Idaho's disclosure law sits on top of local rules. A property condition disclosure form is required from sellers of one to four unit residential property under Idaho Code section 55-2501 and its follow-on sections, with the standard form in section 55-2508. Name known problems plainly, and include work done without a permit.

Sorting records first smooths any sale. In a snowy county, buyers ask about weather wear, so collect these:

  • Your newest Kootenai County tax bill and proof of this year's payments.
  • Permit paperwork, including any use change such as an office or rental.
  • Dates and receipts for roof, furnace and foundation jobs.
  • Your notes for the disclosure form, written in plain terms.
  • Payoff details for any mortgage.

Put a few lines at the top of that folder: who lives in the house, whether anyone rents it, and the date you would like to close. Those three answers shape every offer you receive.

Hand the same folder to a listing agent or a cash buyer and you will get better answers from either one.

Many heirs live elsewhere and have no idea how old the roof or furnace is. A cash sale spares you repeat trips for repairs, cleanouts and showings. The buyer takes the house as it stands, and the title company does the paperwork and pays off any balance from the proceeds.

Check the county tax record early. Unpaid taxes can pile up on a vacant property, and three years of delinquency starts the tax deed process described above. Knowing where the account stands lets you set a closing date with room to spare. A call to the county treasurer will confirm what is owed before you ask anyone for a price.

sections.h2: When a cash sale makes sense
sections.html:
Time or condition is the usual reason. Top price is not.

  • You inherited a house in Kootenai County and live elsewhere.
  • The house needs a roof, a furnace or foundation work that you cannot fund.
  • You are behind on taxes or a mortgage and need to close on a set date.

We buy as-is, and you do not clean, repair or stage. We make an offer after we learn about the house, and you owe nothing if you decline. We do not promise a price before we see the property.

The steps run in order. You describe the house and any money owed on it, we make an offer, and if you accept a title company closes the sale, pays off the mortgage or unpaid taxes from the proceeds and pays you the remainder. Bring your latest tax bill, any permit records and notes on the roof, furnace and foundation to speed it up.

faqs.q: When are Kootenai County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Taxes are due in full on December 20 under Idaho Code 63-903, and owners of real property may pay in two halves. The second half is due June 20.

faqs.q: What happens if I fall three years behind on Post Falls property taxes?
faqs.a: The parcel enters the tax deed process. The owner must pay the third year in full to stop it, or the property can be deeded to Kootenai County.

faqs.q: Which school district is Post Falls in?
faqs.a: The Post Falls School District 273 serves the city. Confirm the boundary for your address with the district.

faqs.q: Do I need to repair my Post Falls house before a cash sale?
faqs.a: No. We buy as-is, so snow damaged roofs, old furnaces and cosmetic wear can stay as they are. You still complete the Idaho property condition disclosure form.

faqs.q: How much snow does Post Falls get?
faqs.a: About 59.3 inches in a typical year, with December and January the snowiest months. Total precipitation averages about 25.7 inches.
